newsitem.title: DUBAI: Ford lifts Gulf sales, but faces strong dollar.
newsitem.headline: Ford lifts Gulf sales, but faces strong dollar.

text.p: A decade since its return to the Middle East, Ford is firming up its market share in the oil-rich Gulf, but now faces a new obstacle to sales growth-- a strong dollar.
"We have had a great year so far. In March we sold 44 percent more vehicles than last March, or a total 1,543," Ford Direct Markets Middle East district manager Jim Benintende said.
First quarter sales were up 17 percent at 3,367, he told Reuters in an interview.
"Our number one obstacle is currency. We have the right products but, at a time when we should be enjoying our biggest growth, we are hampered by currency," he said.
The dollar is currently trading around four-year highs on the yen at around 126 yen, making U.S. exports more expensive.
Ford returned to the Middle East in 1986 after a 25 year-absence because it was on the Arab boycott list.
While Benintende's region also covers Lebanon, Jordan, Syria and Yemen, he said the Gulf's Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain were bigger markets.
Established brand loyalty to other car makers was Ford's second largest hurdle in the region, he said.
"A big problem is getting people to come in and try us. Once we get them in we feel we can provide whatever they need."
Around half the cars on Gulf roads are from Japan, while American manufacturers -- dominated by General Motors -- have around a quarter of the total Gulf car market.

Despite a strong dollar, Benintende expects Middle East sales to grow thanks to Ford's recent entry into the region's small car market, its large Crown Victoria and Grand Marquis sedans' limited local competition and the increasing popularity of sports utility vehicles in the Gulf.
"I see it becoming the biggest export market for Ford Motor Company by 1998. We are hoping to do 22,000 units this year, including Escorts" which are made in Europe, he said.
Ford data show it sold 13,362 vehicles in the region last year, accounting for 4.5 percent of the total market.
The forecast for 1997 is 19,107 North America-sourced vehicles, or 5.9 percent.
Benintende said for the first time since its return, Ford now has a full range of cars and trucks in the Gulf, including the Escort available here only since this year.
"With Caprice pulling out, our Crown Victoria and Grand Marquis sales have grown tremendously," Benintende said. Japanese manufacturers, he said, did not have a similar sized car to compete.
GM last year discontinued the Caprice, the biggest selling American car in the Middle East.
